strengths: The paper introduces S2R-HDR, the first large-scale synthetic HDR fusion dataset (24,000 HDR samples at 1920x1080, ~6x larger than prior datasets), which addresses a real and well-motivated bottleneck in HDR research: collecting ground-truth HDR data for dynamic scenes is costly and limited, especially for extreme scenarios like direct sunlight.

The rendering pipeline design is thoughtful and technically sound: custom UE5 modifications to keep output in linear HDR space (removing baked-in tone mapping), EXR storage to avoid quantization, and camera-shake simulation to mimic handheld capture imperfections.

The dataset provides controllable diversity across motion types (humans, animals, vehicles), indoor/outdoor scenes, and lighting regimes (daylight/twilight/night), with quantitative diversity analysis (seven metrics) and t-SNE distribution comparison against prior real datasets.

The proposed S2R-Adapter (low-rank share branch + high-rank transfer branch) is a plug-and-play design that works with both CNN and Transformer backbones, and supports both supervised fine-tuning and test-time adaptation with unlabeled data via a mean-teacher framework with uncertainty-driven scale factors. It adds no inference overhead when combined with re-reparameterization.

Experiments are comprehensive: three baseline architectures (HDR-Transformer, SCTNet, SAFNet) across two real benchmarks (SCT, Challenge123), both with and without ground truth, plus ablations covering the dataset, each adapter branch, knowledge-forgetting control, and TTA components. Cross-dataset generalization results (Tab. 4) convincingly show that models trained only on the synthetic data outperform models trained on real datasets when transferred, supporting the central claim.

Consistent quantitative improvements over strong recent baselines (e.g., +0.6 to 2 dB PSNR-µ, up to 8.46 dB PSNR-l in the unlabeled setting), supported by qualitative results showing reduced ghosting and better highlight recovery.
The paper is clearly written and well organized, with a detailed supplementary covering implementation details, dataset statistics, and additional experiments.
weaknesses: The S2R-Adapter is largely a combination of existing techniques: LoRA-style low-rank/high-rank adapters, the share/transfer dual-branch structure directly follows ViDA [24], and the mean-teacher TTA with uncertainty-based scaling is also adapted from prior work. The methodological novelty is modest; the main contribution rests on the dataset and its empirical validation.

Dataset quality claims rely heavily on indirect evidence (seven diversity metrics and t-SNE plots). These metrics measure distributional diversity but do not directly establish photometric fidelity of the rendered HDR data against real sensor characteristics (e.g., realistic sensor noise, rolling shutter, radiometric calibration). A direct perceptual/user study or sensor-model validation is missing.

Some experimental comparisons are not fully apples-to-apples: in the main comparison (Tab. 2), 'Ours' is pre-trained on 24,000 synthetic samples plus fine-tuned on the real training set, whereas baselines are trained only on the real training set. The authors do include ablations (Tab. 4) that help disentangle this, but the headline 'state-of-the-art' claims conflate data scale advantage with method advantage.

Several TTA improvements are mixed or small: e.g., SSIM-µ sometimes decreases after TTA (34.93 -> 36.05 in Tab. 6 shows PSNR gains but SSIM-µ drops from 0.9500 to 0.9469), and HDR-VDP2 gains are marginal in some settings (e.g., 68.12 -> 68.40, 57.52 -> 57.38 where it decreases on Challenge123).

The dataset and code release URL is incomplete in the manuscript ('available at' with no link), which weakens reproducibility at submission time; no license, annotation format details, or download size information is given.

Writing and presentation contain avoidable errors (e.g., 'Domain Adaption' in the section title, 'Tesing' in Table 4, 'DHR-VDP2' typo in Table 3, inconsistent figure overlays), suggesting the manuscript needed another careful pass.

The dataset is limited to UE5 rendering with its characteristic look; the paper does not discuss risks that models may latch onto UE5-specific artifacts, nor does it evaluate scene-level generalization beyond the two real benchmarks used.

strengths: The paper addresses a real bottleneck in HDR fusion research: existing ground-truth datasets are tiny (89-144 samples), and a 24,000-sample synthetic dataset rendered in linear HDR (EXR) with controllable motion, lighting, and scenes is a useful community resource.

The custom UE5 rendering pipeline that keeps outputs in linear HDR space (bypassing baked-in tone mapping and gamma correction) is a sensible and non-trivial engineering contribution for making synthetic data usable for HDR tasks.

Experiments are reasonably comprehensive: evaluations with and without ground truth on two standard benchmarks, cross-dataset generalization tests (Tab. 4), and ablations covering the dataset, both adapter branches, knowledge retention, and test-time adaptation components.

The proposed approach achieves consistent PSNR/SSIM improvements over strong recent baselines (SCTNet, SAFNet) when pretraining on S2R-HDR and fine-tuning, and shows good cross-dataset generalization.
The dataset statistics and diversity analysis (seven metrics, t-SNE visualization) attempt to quantitatively support the diversity claims relative to prior datasets.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the S2R-Adapter is essentially a re-application of ViDA [24] (low-rank/high-rank dual-branch adapters, uncertainty-based scaling, mean-teacher EMA) to the HDR fusion task. The design is heavily borrowed, and the paper does not clearly articulate what is new beyond swapping the task domain.

The 'verification' of the two branches relies on t-SNE plots (Fig. 5b), which is weak, qualitative evidence; conclusions about 'knowledge sharing' vs 'knowledge transfer' from such visualizations are over-interpreted.

The domain gap treatment is superficial. The paper addresses tone mapping, gamma, and camera shake, but real raw-sensor characteristics (shot/read noise, CRF, motion blur, rolling shutter) are modeled only crudely — e.g., simple post-hoc Gaussian noise (Supp. A.1) — leaving doubt about how realistic the synthetic-to-real transfer really is.

Inconsistencies and errors undermine confidence: the abstract claims the dataset is 'around 6 times larger than existing ones' but 24,000 vs. 144 is ~166x (the 6x figure appears unexplained); Table 1 is titled 'Qualitative comparison' but is quantitative; typos ('Tesing', 'DHR-VDP2', 'share/shared branch'); the dataset/code URL in the abstract is incomplete ('will be available at' with nothing following), which weakens the reproducibility claim for a dataset paper.

Some claimed contributions are questionable: the claim of being the 'first large-scale' HDR dataset sits uneasily with the existence of Real-HDRV [37], which the authors themselves acknowledge as 'the largest'; this positioning needs to be more precise (synthetic, ground-truth fusion) or softened.

Gains are mixed in magnitude: on SCT with ground truth, the HDR-VDP2 improvement is only 0.11 (69.33 vs 69.22) for SCTNet w S2R, and in Table 3 on Challenge123 the TTA adapter actually slightly hurts SAFNet (57.38 vs 57.52 without adaptation), contradicting the narrative that test-time adaptation consistently helps. These cases deserve analysis rather than silence.

The comparison in Table 3 is somewhat apples-to-oranges: baselines are trained only on small real datasets while the proposed method additionally uses 24,000 synthetic samples plus test-time adaptation; a fairer analysis of where the gains come from (data scale vs. adapter design) is only partially provided via Table 4/5.

Overall clarity needs improvement: the method section is readable, but the paper's central claim ('achieves state-of-the-art') rests on modest margins over the two baseline architectures it fine-tunes, and the significance of the adapter contribution beyond its source work is not convincingly established.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: existing HDR fusion datasets are small (89-144 samples), and ground-truth capture is genuinely difficult; a large-scale synthetic dataset is a reasonable and useful response.

The S2R-HDR dataset is a substantial contribution: 24,000 HDR samples (~6x larger than prior work), with thoughtful rendering pipeline details (linear HDR output in EXR, modified tone mapping/gamma, camera shake simulation, flexible LDR exposure synthesis).

Comprehensive evaluation: multiple strong baselines spanning CNN and transformer architectures (SAFNet, SCTNet, HDR-Transformer), evaluation on both labeled and unlabeled settings, cross-dataset generalization experiments, and multiple ablations (branches, scale factors, knowledge forgetting, TTA components).

The demonstration that models trained solely on S2R-HDR generalize better across SCT and Challenge123 than models trained directly on either real dataset (Tab. 4) is a convincing piece of evidence for the dataset's value.

The S2R-Adapter is practical: plug-and-play, architecture-agnostic, and zero inference overhead via re-parameterization; the uncertainty-based dynamic scaling of shared/transfer branches is a sensible design for test-time adaptation.

Diversity analysis using seven established metrics and t-SNE visualization provides quantitative support for the claimed dataset characteristics, and the supplementary provides useful dataset statistics and additional experiments.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty on the adaptation side: S2R-Adapter is essentially a combination of known components (LoRA-style low-rank adapters, high-rank adapters, mean-teacher TTA, uncertainty-based scaling largely following ViDA [24]), and the paper does not clearly delineate what is new versus inherited.

The dataset diversity metrics (Tab. 1) measure properties like dynamic range extent and colorfulness, which are naturally easier to satisfy with synthetic rendering; they do not measure photorealism or sensor realism, so the claim that the dataset 'simulates a broad range of real-world environments' is only partially supported. Sensor noise modeling is simplistic (Gaussian noise only).

Comparison fairness: the main results (Tab. 2) compare models pre-trained on 24k synthetic images plus fine-tuning against baselines trained only on the small real datasets; the ablation showing S2R-HDR pre-training (rather than just larger-scale pre-training in general) is beneficial would be strengthened by e.g. pre-training on combined real datasets or other synthetic sources.

Some reported gains are small or inconsistent (e.g., marginal SSIM differences in Tab. 2, HDR-VDP2 of 69.33 vs. 69.22 for SCTNet), and Table 3 contains typos ('DHR-VDP2') suggesting less than careful preparation.

Reproducibility concerns: the dataset/code release URL is a placeholder in the submission ('Dataset and code will be available at'), and no discussion of the licensing of UE5 marketplace assets (humans, vehicles, animals) used for rendering, which matters for a dataset release.
Evaluation sets are very small (36 and 27 test samples), so several decibel-level claims rest on limited data; statistical significance or variance across seeds is not reported.
No user study or perceptual evaluation beyond HDR-VDP2, despite the paper's emphasis on visual quality of tone-mapped outputs.

strengths: S2R-HDR is the first large-scale synthetic HDR fusion dataset (24,000 EXR frames at 1920×1080 with ground-truth HDR, auxiliary flow/depth/normal data), addressing a genuine data bottleneck in the field; the scale (~166x) and diversity (humans, animals, vehicles; indoor/outdoor; day/twilight/night) are a real contribution.

The rendering pipeline is thoughtfully designed: removing baked-in tone mapping to keep linear HDR, floating-point EXR storage, and Perlin-noise-based camera shake simulation show attention to making synthetic data usable for HDR tasks.

Experiments are extensive and multi-faceted: supervised adaptation on SCT and Challenge123, test-time adaptation without ground truth, cross-dataset generalization (Table 4), comparisons against additional real datasets (Kalantari, Real-HDRV), an HDR video reconstruction task, temporal consistency, and TTA runtime analysis.

Meaningful quantitative gains (up to ~2dB PSNR-µ on Challenge123; strong TTA improvements, e.g., +8.46dB PSNR-ℓ on SCT), supported by thorough ablations of the adapter branches, scale factors, teacher-student framework, and uncertainty-based scaling, plus a knowledge-forgetting analysis (Table 7).
The method is architecture-agnostic (applied to both CNN-based SAFNet and transformer-based SCTNet) and the adapter is claimed to be mergeable via reparameterization with no inference overhead.
Dataset, code, and a detailed generation pipeline (Appendix A.9) are released, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: The S2R-Adapter itself is methodologically incremental: it largely combines existing components (LoRA-style low/high-rank adapters from ViDA, uncertainty-based scaling from SAR/Tent-style TTA, mean-teacher EMA from Tarvainen & Valpola) rather than introducing a fundamentally new technique; the novelty rests mainly on task-specific adaptation choices.

The core sim-to-real problem is only partially solved: models trained purely on S2R-HDR still perform substantially worse on real data (e.g., 34.89 vs 42.55 PSNR-µ on SCT), so the practical recipe always requires adaptation to real data; sensor realism is limited (Gaussian noise injection is simplistic; no rolling shutter, quantization, or realistic noise modeling), and the abstract's claim of achieving SOTA only holds with the adaptation component.
Evaluation relies on very small real test sets (36 and 27 samples), where ~0.3-0.6dB differences may not be statistically robust; no significance testing or error bars are provided.

The dataset diversity comparison (Table 1, t-SNE analysis) uses global statistics that may favor rendered content without strongly demonstrating cross-domain transferability beyond the downstream results.

The pretrain-on-synthetic + adapt-on-real pipelines are not strictly comparable to baselines trained directly on real data (more total data is consumed), which is acknowledged but makes headline comparisons somewhat favorable; MUSIQ-based evaluations (Table 13) are non-reference and weak evidence.

The reproducibility statement contains a placeholder ('available at URL:'), and some dataset details (licensing of purchased UE5 assets, exact exposure selection strategy across sequences) are under-specified for full community reuse.
Several ablation gains are small (e.g., learned vs fixed scale factors, Unc component adding ~0.2dB), so the adaptive-scaling design is not strongly justified relative to its complexity.

strengths: The S2R-HDR dataset addresses a genuine scalability bottleneck in HDR fusion: existing ground-truth datasets contain only ~90-150 samples, and a 24,000-sample synthetic dataset with auxiliary modalities (optical flow, depth, normals) is a real and reusable community resource.

The evaluation is reasonably extensive: results on two recent real benchmarks (SCT, Challenge123), two architecture families (CNN and transformer), a supervised adaptation setting, a test-time adaptation setting, additional experiments on Kalantari/Real-HDRV/video reconstruction, and multiple ablations (branch design, scale factors, knowledge forgetting, TTA components).

The cross-dataset generalization analysis (Table 4) is informative and directly demonstrates the limited generalization of models trained on small real datasets, supporting the paper's core motivation.
The rendering pipeline design choices (linear HDR output, EXR storage, camera shake simulation, exposure augmentation from raw HDR sequences) are sensible and well-motivated for the HDR task.
weaknesses: The methodological contribution (S2R-Adapter) is incremental: it is essentially a combination of existing components — dual-rank LoRA-style adapters with share/transfer branches following VIDA (Liu et al., 2023a), uncertainty-based scale adjustment from prior TTA work, and a standard mean-teacher framework. The paper does not clearly articulate what is new beyond re-instantiating these ideas for HDR fusion.

The sim-to-real realism argument is under-developed for the HDR domain. Rendered UE5 imagery lacks key sensor characteristics (real noise modeling beyond ad-hoc additive Gaussian noise, sensor CRF, quantization, rolling shutter, motion blur physics), and the paper only briefly discusses the texture-level domain gap. Given that HDR fusion is a low-level imaging task, this gap matters more than the paper acknowledges.

The fairness of headline comparisons is questionable: in Table 2 the proposed methods benefit from large-scale synthetic pretraining plus adaptation, while baselines are trained only on ~100-sample real sets. The ablation shows plain fine-tuning achieves nearly the same result as S2R-Adapter (43.03 vs 43.33 PSNR-µ on SCT), so the adapter's added value over the dataset alone is small.

Generalization results are mixed and selectively framed: in Table 3, models trained on S2R-HDR alone are often worse in PSNR-µ than baselines (e.g., 34.83 vs 35.14), with gains concentrated in PSNR-ℓ (e.g., +8.46dB), which is anomalous and not explained; in Table 14, S2R-HDR training underperforms Vimeo+Sintel and Real-HDRV baselines on video reconstruction. The text claims state-of-the-art generalization without adequately reconciling these inconsistencies.

Reproducibility is weakened by a placeholder in the paper: the code/dataset URL is literally left as 'URL:' in the reproducibility statement, and part of the pipeline depends on purchased UE5 assets whose redistribution rights are not discussed.
Presentation issues undermine polish: 'Domain Adaption' section title typo, incomplete sentence in the abstract (the dataset/code link is cut off), and Table 9 contains metric typos ('PNSR').

Some ablation gains are marginal and within plausible noise: e.g., MUSIQ differences in Table 13 are ~0.3-1.5 points, and the learned scale factors in Table 5 add ~0.05dB, yet these are presented as evidence of design effectiveness without statistical significance analysis.

strengths: The S2R-HDR dataset addresses a genuine and well-motivated bottleneck in HDR fusion: the extremely small size of existing ground-truth datasets (89-144 samples). A 24,000-image rendered dataset with linear-space EXR output, auxiliary modalities (optical flow, depth, normals), and controllable lighting/motion is a substantial community resource.

The evaluation is unusually thorough: comparisons across two recent benchmarks (SCT, Challenge123), three baseline architectures (CNN- and transformer-based), a cross-dataset generalization study (Table 4), ablations of each adapter branch, knowledge-forgetting analysis (Table 7), test-time adaptation ablations (Table 6), runtime analysis (Table 17), and additional experiments on Kalantari, Sen, Tursun, and HDR video reconstruction datasets in the appendix.

The domain gap is honestly acknowledged and quantitatively characterized (t-SNE analysis, difference maps in Figure 9), and the two-branch (shared low-rank / transfer high-rank) adapter design with uncertainty-driven scale factors is a sensible, well-executed solution that plugs into multiple architectures.
Results are convincing in the key experiments: ~2dB PSNR-µ gains on Challenge123 and clear advantages in test-time adaptation without ground truth (Table 3), supporting the central claims.
Reproducibility is addressed with detailed hyperparameters (Appendix A.1), a complete rendering pipeline description (A.9), and a code/dataset release statement.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty of S2R-Adapter is incremental: it is essentially the ViDA-style dual-rank adapter (Liu et al., 2023a) combined with mean-teacher TTA and uncertainty-based scaling, all established techniques. The paper's main contribution is the dataset and its empirical validation, not a new adaptation algorithm; positioning as a 'novel domain adaptation method' (Conclusion) overstates this.

The domain gap remains substantial: models trained only on S2R-HDR perform poorly on SCT (34.89 vs 42.55 PSNR-µ, Table 4), so the reported SOTA results depend heavily on fine-tuning/adaptation on real data. The paper should temper the 'achieves state-of-the-art' framing and clarify that the benefit is better pretraining + efficient adaptation, not synthetic-data-only training.

Some experimental inconsistencies reduce confidence: e.g., 'Dataset and code are available at URL:' is a placeholder on page 1; Figure 12's caption says 'Distribution of optical flow directions' but shows the rendering pipeline (the flow figure is Figure 13); Table 17 reports 43.85/47.23 PSNR values that do not match Table 3/Table 5 numbers for the same setting (34.89/36.28); Table 3 lists 'DHR-VDP2'; Table 9 has 'PNSR' typos.

The headline comparison (Table 2) is somewhat confounded: baselines are trained on ~100-120 real samples while the proposed models are pretrained on 24,000 synthetic images plus adaptation. Although Table 4 partially disentangles dataset vs. adapter effects, an additional control (e.g., baselines trained with an equal number of augmented real samples, or comparisons against synthetic augmentation baselines like GTA-HDR) would strengthen the claim.

Sensor realism of the rendered data is only partially addressed: Gaussian noise injection is a simplified proxy for real sensor noise/CRF, and there is no user study or perceptual validation of the rendered HDR quality beyond no-reference MUSIQ.

The rank setting rt ≥ max(hin, hout) for the 'transfer branch' makes it a full-rank (essentially full fine-tuning) residual; its parameter cost relative to plain fine-tuning is not reported, and ablation gains of the learned scale factors (Table 5, last row) are marginal (~0.01-0.05 dB), which weakens the significance of that design element.
